assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstrations of record accuracy and stability, turned atomic spectroscopy into a precision tool that probes time, relativity and fundamental constants at the 1e-18 level. This is an atomic-physics result I can judge directly: the physics is clear, the agreement between independent laboratories is exceptional, and the work builds on earlier combs and laser cooling prizes in a way that adds something new.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice idea and made early demonstrations in strontium; Ye's JILA group brought the clock to the highest accuracy and used it for gravitational redshift tests on millimetre scales. Two names give a clean configuration, though other groups (for example Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow-era NIST colleagues) made real contributions and a purist may argue about the lattice-clock versus single-ion clock priority.
assessment.maturity: Many laboratories worldwide have independently reproduced and improved the clocks, and comparisons across institutes are routine. The field is mature, with redefinition of the second under discussion, so recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee judges clocks as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 AMO prizes rather than a new discovery.
Relative weight of single-ion clocks (Wineland-era) versus lattice clocks is something I have not verified in detail.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the superfluid to Mott insulator transition to single-atom-resolved quantum gas microscopes, gives controllable many-body systems where one can see quantum matter directly. It is fundamental, conceptually clear, and has changed how many-body problems are studied.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and collaborators) supplied the theoretical proposal for the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch carried out the decisive Mott insulator experiments and the microscopy. Cirac is credited and was central to quantum simulation concepts, but the list allows only three and I favour the proposal plus the two key experimental leaders. Jaksch, a key originator of the lattice proposal, is not among the supplied names, an allocation issue the list cannot resolve.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by dozens of groups and the basis of a large field, so very mature. Possible overlap with the 2001 and 1997 cold-atom prizes is acceptable.
uncertainties: Fair allocation among four credited names plus uncredited theorists such as Jaksch.
Boundary with a separate Cirac-Zoller quantum computing candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Geometric and topological phases, the Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's phase, reveal that quantum mechanics carries global information that local fields do not. This is unexpected, deep and underlies much of modern atomic, molecular and condensed matter theory, including topological band theory. It speaks directly to the question of what is physically real in the quantum world.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov (with Bohm, who is deceased) and Berry are the clear central figures. Pancharatnam and Bohm are historically relevant but cannot be named; the two names supplied form a natural pair, though the Aharonov-Bohm effect without Bohm is awkward.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed for decades, in optics, NMR, neutrons and solid-state systems. The recognition is arguably overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Posthumous credit to David Bohm and Pancharatnam cannot be reflected.
Whether the committee treats this as a theoretical discovery with enough experimental discovery character.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bringing mechanical oscillators of macroscopic size into their quantum ground state and entangled or squeezed states addresses the question I find most compelling, where the boundary between the quantum and classical worlds lies. The experiments are elegant and the control precision is impressive.
assessment.attribution: Cleland made the first quantum ground-state mechanical resonator coupled to a qubit; Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg developed cavity optomechanics and ground-state cooling. Other leaders (Lehnert, Teufel, Painter, Schwab) also made decisive contributions, so a three-name prize would leave out comparable work.
assessment.maturity: Several independent groups confirm ground-state cooling, entanglement and squeezing, but the field is still evolving and application-independent landmarks keep arriving; the most recent prize on macroscopic circuit tunnelling may make this feel adjacent.
uncertainties: Credit is diffuse among several optomechanics groups.
Overlap in spirit with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of flat bands at magic angles, and the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, opened moire quantum materials, a genuinely unexpected new platform with a simple geometric origin.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald gave the continuum-model prediction of the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery. This combination of theory and experiment is a natural fit. Cao and Yankowitz co-authors and other theorists (Santos, Lopes dos Santos, Peres) will raise credit questions.
assessment.maturity: Replicated widely and a large field has grown in a few years, but understanding of the superconducting mechanism is not settled, so some may judge it a bit early.
uncertainties: Priority questions among theorists and student authors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of Rydberg atoms combine single-atom control with strong interactions, enabling quantum simulation of many-body states and entangling gates. As a theorist of Rydberg and atomic structure I appreciate the physics, which is clear and well understood.
assessment.attribution: Lukin led the large programmable arrays and many-body experiments, Browaeys the early tweezer-array and interaction work, and Saffman the blockade gate proposals and demonstrations. The three names are reasonable, with Bernien, Endres, Weiss and others adjacent.
assessment.maturity: Several independent groups reproduce key results, but the field is moving fast and the lasting scientific discovery may be clearer in a few years.
uncertainties: Whether the fundamental discovery is separable from the engineering of quantum computing platforms.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and its realisation by Blatt and others is a foundational result for quantum information and ion control. The physics is clean and precisely understood, though the 2012 prize to Wineland already honoured ion control.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the scheme; Blatt realised gates and entanglement in Innsbruck. Wineland's NIST work and Monroe are major contributors, and the 2012 prize overlaps. Cirac and Zoller also appear in other candidates, which complicates the allocation.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently verified, though the technological promise of large-scale quantum computing is still unrealised.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with other Cirac-Zoller candidates.
Whether this is recognised as a discovery or a technological proposal.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics realises strong light-matter coupling on a chip and underlies superconducting quantum processors. It is a conceptually elegant extension of cavity QED, which I know well, with a large impact on measurement of quantum systems.
assessment.attribution: Blais (theory), Wallraff and Schoelkopf (experiments) are the natural trio, though Devoret and Martinis and collaborators complicate things, as does the 2025 prize concerning circuit quantum behaviour.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many laboratories and technologically significant, but the 2025 prize reduces the timeliness of another superconducting circuit award.
uncertainties: Credit relative to other superconducting-qubit pioneers.
